claim: Metal-ion-dependent nucleases play crucial roles in cellular defense and biotechnological applications.
source: Metal-ion-dependent nucleases play crucial roles in cellular defense and biotechnological applications.
evidence: This is a general statement about the biological and technological importance of metal-ion-dependent nucleases, representing established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Time-resolved crystallography has resolved catalytic details of metal-ion-dependent DNA hydrolysis and synthesis, uncovering the essential roles of multiple metal ions during catalysis.
source: Time-resolved crystallography has resolved catalytic details of metal-ion-dependent DNA hydrolysis and synthesis, uncovering the essential roles of multiple metal ions during catalysis.
evidence: This statement references prior work in the field using time-resolved crystallography, supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The histidine-metal (His-Me) superfamily nucleases bind one divalent metal ion and require a conserved histidine to promote catalysis.
source: The histidine-metal (His-Me) superfamily nucleases are renowned for binding one divalent metal ion and requiring a conserved histidine to promote catalysis.
evidence: This is a characterization of His-Me nucleases based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: Many His-Me family nucleases, including homing endonucleases and Cas9 nuclease, have been adapted for biotechnological and biomedical applications.
source: Many His-Me family nucleases, including homing endonucleases and Cas9 nuclease, have been adapted for biotechnological and biomedical applications.
evidence: This statement reflects established knowledge about the applications of His-Me nucleases in biotechnology and medicine.

claim: Only one divalent metal ion is required during I-PpoI catalysis.
source: By observing DNA hydrolysis in crystallo with His-Me I-PpoI nuclease as a model system, we proved that only one divalent metal ion is required during its catalysis.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data from in crystallo observations and metal ion soaking experiments.

claim: Several possible deprotonation pathways exist for the nucleophilic water in I-PpoI catalysis.
source: Moreover, we uncovered several possible deprotonation pathways for the nucleophilic water.
evidence: This finding is supported by mutagenesis experiments and structural observations presented in the manuscript.

claim: Binding of the single metal ion and water deprotonation are concerted during I-PpoI catalysis.
source: Interestingly, binding of the single metal ion and water deprotonation are concerted during catalysis.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from experimental observations showing correlation between metal ion binding and pH effects on catalysis.

claim: The catalytic mechanism of His-Me nucleases is distinct from multi-metal-ion-dependent DNA polymerases and nucleases.
source: Our results reveal catalytic details of His-Me nucleases, which is distinct from multi-metal-ion-dependent DNA polymerases and nucleases.
evidence: This is a comparative conclusion based on the experimental findings and comparison with known mechanisms of other enzymes.

claim: Mg2+-dependent nucleases play fundamental roles in DNA replication and repair.
source: Mg2+-dependent nucleases play fundamental roles in DNA replication and repair (Kao and Bambara, 2003; Shen et al., 2005; Marti and Fleck, 2004; Mimitou and Symington, 2009)
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Mg2+-dependent nucleases are involved in RNA processing.
source: Mg2+-dependent nucleases play fundamental roles in...RNA processing (Patel and Steitz, 2003; Abelson et al., 1998; Chu and Rana, 2007; Moore and Proudfoot, 2009)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Mg2+-dependent nucleases are involved in immune response and defense.
source: Mg2+-dependent nucleases play fundamental roles in...immune response and defense (James et al., 1996; Sorek et al., 2008; Tock and Dryden, 2005)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Mg2+-dependent nucleases are widely employed for genome editing in biotechnological and biomedical applications.
source: Moreover, they are widely employed for genome editing in biotechnological and biomedical applications (Adli, 2018; Carroll, 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Mg2+-dependent nucleases cleave DNA through a SN2-type reaction.
source: These nucleases are proposed to cleave DNA through a SN2-type reaction, in which a water molecule, or sometimes, a tyrosine side chain (Grindley et al., 2006), initiates the nucleophilic attack on the scissile phosphate with the help of metal ions (Yang, 2011).
evidence: This is a mechanistic proposal supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Metal ions can orient and stabilize the binding of the negatively charged nucleic acid backbone.
source: Metal ions can orient and stabilize the binding of the negatively charged nucleic acid backbone (Chen et al., 2017)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Metal ions promote proton transfer, nucleophilic attack, and stabilization of the transition state in nuclease catalysis.
source: Metal ions can orient and stabilize the binding of the negatively charged nucleic acid backbone (Chen et al., 2017), promoting proton transfer, nucleophilic attack, and stabilization of the transition state.
evidence: This is a general mechanistic statement supported by citation and established knowledge.

claim: Mg2+-dependent nucleases can be categorized by the number of metal ions captured in their active site.
source: As a highly varied family of enzymes, Mg2+-dependent nucleases can be broadly categorized by the number of metal ions captured in their active site.
evidence: This is a classification statement based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: Mg2+-dependent nucleases with one and two metal ions have been observed.
source: So far, Mg2+-dependent nucleases with one and two metal ions have been observed.
evidence: This statement reflects established knowledge from previous structural studies.

claim: In two-Mg2+-ion-dependent nucleases, one metal ion binds on the leaving group side of the scissile phosphate (Me2+B) while the other binds on the nucleophile side (Me2+A).
source: In the two-Mg2+-ion-dependent nuclease, a metal ion binds on the leaving group side of the scissile phosphate (Me2+B) while the other binds on the nucleophile side (Me2+A).
evidence: This is a description of the two-metal-ion mechanism based on established knowledge.

claim: In one-metal-ion-dependent nucleases, only the metal ion corresponding to the B site in two-metal-ion-dependent nucleases is present.
source: In one-metal-ion-dependent nucleases, only the metal ion corresponding to the B site in two-metal-ion-dependent nucleases is present (Yang, 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Transiently bound metal ions have been identified in RNaseH via time-resolved X-ray crystallography.
source: Moreover, transiently bound metal ions have been identified in the previously thought two-metal-ion RNaseH (Samara and Yang, 2018)...via time-resolved X-ray crystallography
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a specific study.

claim: Transiently bound metal ions have been identified in EndoV nucleases via time-resolved X-ray crystallography.
source: Moreover, transiently bound metal ions have been identified in...EndoV nucleases (Wu et al., 2019) via time-resolved X-ray crystallography
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a specific study.

claim: Transiently bound metal ions play key roles in various stages of RNaseH and EndoV catalysis.
source: Moreover, transiently bound metal ions have been identified in the previously thought two-metal-ion RNaseH (Samara and Yang, 2018) and EndoV nucleases (Wu et al., 2019) via time-resolved X-ray crystallography, proposed to play key roles in various stages of their catalysis.
evidence: This is a mechanistic proposal based on cited studies.

claim: Catalysis in the one-metal-ion-dependent APE1 nuclease has been observed in crystallo.
source: Similarly, catalysis in the one-metal-ion-dependent APE1 nuclease has been observed in crystallo, but mechanistic details regarding its metal-ion dependence have not been thoroughly explored (Freudenthal et al., 2015; Whitaker et al., 2018; Dupureur, 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Three-Zn2+-dependent nucleases exist with two Zn2+ binding in the A- and B-equivalent positions, while the third Zn2+ coordinates the sp oxygen on the nucleophile side of the scissile phosphate.
source: There also exist three-Zn2+-dependent nucleases, with two Zn2+ binding in the A- and B-equivalent positions, while the third Zn2+ coordinating the sp oxygen on the nucleophile side of the scissile phosphate (Garcin et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a specific study.

claim: It remains unclear how the single metal ion in one-metal-ion-dependent nucleases aligns the substrate, promotes deprotonation and nucleophilic attack, and stabilizes the pentacovalent transition state.
source: However, it remains unclear how the single metal ion in one-metal-ion-dependent nucleases is capable of aligning the substrate, promoting deprotonation and nucleophilic attack, and stabilizing the pentacovalent transition state.
evidence: This identifies a knowledge gap in the field that the study aims to address.

claim: His-Me nucleases perform critical tasks in apoptosis.
source: A large subfamily of one-metal-ion-dependent nucleases consist of histidine-metal (His-Me) nucleases that perform critical tasks in biological pathways such as apoptosis (Arnoult et al., 2003; Lin et al., 2016)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: His-Me nucleases perform critical tasks in extracellular defense.
source: A large subfamily of one-metal-ion-dependent nucleases consist of histidine-metal (His-Me) nucleases that perform critical tasks in biological pathways such as...extracellular defense (Cheng et al., 2002; Hsia et al., 2004)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: His-Me nucleases perform critical tasks in intracellular immunity (CRISPR–Cas9).
source: A large subfamily of one-metal-ion-dependent nucleases consist of histidine-metal (His-Me) nucleases that perform critical tasks in biological pathways such as...intracellular immunity (CRISPR–Cas9) (Doudna and Charpentier, 2014; Ran et al., 2013)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: His-Me nucleases perform critical tasks in intron homing (homing endonuclease).
source: A large subfamily of one-metal-ion-dependent nucleases consist of histidine-metal (His-Me) nucleases that perform critical tasks in biological pathways such as...intron homing (homing endonuclease) (Chevalier and Stoddard, 2001; Stoddard, 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The structural cores and active sites of His-Me nucleases are highly conserved despite sharing poor sequence homology.
source: Despite sharing poor sequence homology, the structural cores and active sites of His-Me nucleases are highly conserved
evidence: This is a structural observation based on established knowledge from previous studies.

claim: His-Me nucleases are proposed to catalyze DNA hydrolysis through a similar mechanism.
source: Despite sharing poor sequence homology, the structural cores and active sites of His-Me nucleases are highly conserved and thus are proposed to catalyze DNA hydrolysis through a similar mechanism (Yang, 2011; Stoddard, 2005; Wu et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a mechanistic proposal supported by citations to previous work.

claim: His-Me nucleases active sites are surrounded by two beta sheets and an alpha helix.
source: Surrounded by two beta sheets and an alpha helix, the His-Me nucleases active sites all contain a single metal ion, a histidine, and an asparagine
evidence: This is a structural description supported by structural data shown in figures.

claim: His-Me nucleases active sites contain a single metal ion, a histidine, and an asparagine.
source: Surrounded by two beta sheets and an alpha helix, the His-Me nucleases active sites all contain a single metal ion, a histidine, and an asparagine (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, and Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This structural feature is supported by structural data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: The asparagine residue in His-Me nucleases helps to stabilize metal ion binding.
source: The asparagine residue helps to stabilize metal ion binding
evidence: This is a functional assignment based on structural observations and established knowledge.

claim: The strictly conserved histidine in His-Me nucleases is suggested to deprotonate a nearby water for nucleophilic attack toward the scissile phosphate.
source: whereas the strictly conserved histidine is suggested to deprotonate a nearby water for nucleophilic attack toward the scissile phosphate (Galburt et al., 1999; Pommer et al., 2001; Li et al., 2003; Shen et al., 2004).
evidence: This mechanistic proposal is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The dynamic reaction process of DNA hydrolysis by His-Me nucleases has never been visualized.
source: To this day, the dynamic reaction process of DNA hydrolysis by His-Me nucleases has never been visualized
evidence: This identifies a gap in the field prior to this study.

claim: The mechanism of single metal-ion-dependent and histidine-promoted catalysis in His-Me nucleases remains unclear.
source: and the mechanism of single metal-ion-dependent and histidine-promoted catalysis remains unclear.
evidence: This identifies a knowledge gap that the study aims to address.

claim: CRISPR–Cas9 is important for genome editing and disease treatment.
source: Emerging genome editing and disease treatment involving CRISPR–Cas9 emphasize the importance of understanding the catalytic mechanism of DNA hydrolysis by His-Me nucleases (Schwank et al., 2013; Sharma et al., 2021; Khan et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work on CRISPR applications.

claim: Recent crystal and cryo-electron microscope structures of Cas9 have captured the His-Me family Cas9 HNH active site engaged with DNA before and after cleavage.
source: Recent crystal and cryo-electron microscope structures of Cas9 have captured the His-Me family Cas9 histidine–asparagine–histidine (HNH) active site engaged with DNA before and after cleavage (Sun et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2020; Zhu et al., 2019; Das et al., 2023).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to recent structural studies.

claim: Key catalytic details of Cas9, such as metal ion dependence, transition-state stabilization, and alternative deprotonation pathways, remain elusive due to relatively low resolution and static nature of the structures.
source: However, due to the relatively low resolution and the static nature of the structures, key catalytic details, such as metal ion dependence, transition-state stabilization, and alternative deprotonation pathways, remain elusive.
evidence: This is an assessment of limitations in previous Cas9 structural studies.

claim: The large size and multiple conformational checkpoints during Cas9 catalysis hinder in crystallo observation of Cas9 catalysis.
source: Moreover, the large size and multiple conformational checkpoints during Cas9 catalysis (Sun et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2020; Zhu et al., 2019; Das et al., 2023) hinder in crystallo observation of Cas9 catalysis.
evidence: This statement explains technical challenges with Cas9 studies, supported by citations.

claim: I-PpoI is a well-characterized intron-encoded homing endonuclease member of the physarum polycephalum slimemold.
source: I-PpoI is a well-characterized intron-encoded homing endonuclease member of the physarum polycephalum slimemold.
evidence: This is a description of the model system used in the study.

claim: By 1999, Stoddard and colleagues captured intermediate structures of I-PpoI complexed with DNA before and after product formation.
source: By 1999, Stoddard and colleagues were able to capture intermediate structures of I-PpoI complexed with DNA before and after product formation (Galburt et al., 1999; Flick et al., 1998).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous structural studies.

claim: Over 40 atomic resolution structures of I-PpoI were determined during its reaction process.
source: By determining over 40 atomic resolution structures of I-PpoI during its reaction process, we show that one and only one divalent metal ion is involved in DNA hydrolysis.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach and data collection in the study.

claim: Metal ion binding and water deprotonation are highly concerted during I-PpoI catalysis.
source: Notably, metal ion binding and water deprotonation are highly concerted during catalysis.
evidence: This is a mechanistic conclusion based on experimental observations.

claim: The findings provide mechanistic insights into one-metal-ion-dependent nucleases.
source: Our findings provide mechanistic insights into one-metal-ion-dependent nucleases, enhancing future design and engineering of these enzymes for emerging biomedical applications.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the study's contributions.

claim: A complex of I-PpoI and a palindromic DNA was crystallized at pH 6 with 0.2 M sodium malonate.
source: First, a complex of I-PpoI and a palindromic DNA was crystalized at pH 6 with 0.2 M sodium malonate.
evidence: This describes the experimental crystallization conditions.

claim: A dimer of I-PpoI was found in the asymmetric unit, with both active sites engaged for catalysis and DNA in the middle bent by 55°.
source: Similar to previous studies, a dimer of I-PpoI was found in the asymmetric unit, with both active sites engaged for catalysis and DNA in the middle bent by 55° (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a structural observation from crystallographic data.

claim: The two I-PpoI molecules in the asymmetric unit were almost identical and served as internal controls for evaluating the reaction process.
source: The two I-PpoI molecules were almost identical and thus served as internal controls for evaluating the reaction process (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This describes the experimental design using the crystal structure.

claim: Within each I-PpoI active site, a water molecule (nucleophilic water, WatN) existed 3.6 Å from the scissile phosphate, near the imidazole side chain of His98.
source: Within each I-PpoI active site, a water molecule (nucleophilic water, WatN) existed 3.6 Å from the scissile phosphate, near the imidazole side chain of His98.
evidence: This is a structural observation from crystallographic data.

claim: On the leaving group side of the scissile phosphate, the metal exhibited an octahedral geometry, being coordinated by three water molecules, two oxygen atoms from the scissile phosphate, and the conserved asparagine.
source: On the leaving group side of the scissile phosphate, the metal exhibited an octahedral geometry, being coordinated by three water molecules, two oxygen atoms from the scissile phosphate, and the conserved asparagine (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a structural observation from crystallographic data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Malonate was removed from the crystallization buffer by equilibrating the crystals in 200 mM NaCl buffer at pH 6, 7, or 8 for 30 min.
source: Next, we removed malonate in the crystallization buffer, which may chelate metal ions and hinder metal ion diffusion (Deerfield et al., 1991), by equilibrating the crystals in 200 mM NaCl buffer at pH 6, 7, or 8 for 30 min.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure for preparing crystals for metal ion soaking.

claim: Malonate may chelate metal ions and hinder metal ion diffusion.
source: Next, we removed malonate in the crystallization buffer, which may chelate metal ions and hinder metal ion diffusion (Deerfield et al., 1991)
evidence: This is a rationale for the experimental design, supported by a citation.

claim: The diffraction quality of the crystals was not affected during the soaking.
source: The diffraction quality of the crystals was not affected during the soaking.
evidence: This is an experimental observation about crystal quality.

claim: The structures of I-PpoI equilibrated at pH 6, 7, or 8 in the presence of 200 mM NaCl showed no signs of product formation and appeared similar to the malonate and previous reported I-PpoI structures.
source: The structures of I-PpoI equilibrated at pH 6, 7, or 8 in the presence of 200 mM NaCl showed no signs of product formation and appeared similar to the malonate and previous reported I-PpoI structures (Galburt et al., 1999; Flick et al., 1998; Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is a structural observation from crystallographic data.

claim: Soaking I-PpoI crystals in buffer containing Tl+ resulted in anomalous electron density at the metal ion-binding site without product formation.
source: To confirm if a monovalent metal ion binds in the pre-reaction state, we soaked the I-PpoI crystals in buffer containing Tl+ and detected anomalous electron density at the metal ion-binding site without product formation (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from anomalous diffraction data.

claim: Monovalent metal ion can bind within the I-PpoI active site without initiating reaction.
source: Our results support that the monovalent metal ion can bind within the active site without initiating reaction, in corroboration with our biochemical assays (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This conclusion is supported by both structural and biochemical data.

claim: After 600 s soaking in 500 µM Mg2+, a significant negative Fo − Fc peak on the leaving group side of the scissile phosphate atom and a positive Fo − Fc peak on the other side were observed, indicating that DNA hydrolysis was occurring in crystallo.
source: After 600 s soaking, we saw a significant negative Fo − Fc peak on the leaving group side of the scissile phosphate atom as well as a positive Fo − Fc peak on the other side (Figure 1—figure supplement 3D), indicating that DNA hydrolysis was occurring in crystallo.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from electron density maps indicating chemical reaction.

claim: After DNA cleavage, the newly generated phosphate group shifted 1 Å toward the WatN.
source: After DNA cleavage, the newly generated phosphate group shifted 1 Å toward the WatN (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a structural observation from crystallographic data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: An additional product state was observed after soaking the crystals in 500 µM Mg2+ for 600 and 1800 s, at which the newly formed phosphate shifted 3 Å away from the metal ion to form a hydrogen bond with Arg61.
source: Furthermore, an additional product state was observed after soaking the crystals in 500 µM Mg2+ for 600 and 1800 s, at which the newly formed phosphate shifted 3 Å away from the metal ion to form a hydrogen bond with Arg61 (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is a structural observation from crystallographic data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The implementation of I-PpoI with in crystallo Me2+ soaking is feasible for observing the I-PpoI catalytic process and dissecting the mechanism of His-Me nucleases.
source: Our results confirm that the implementation of I-PpoI with in crystallo Me2+ soaking is feasible for observing the I-PpoI catalytic process and dissecting the mechanism of His-Me nucleases.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the successful observation of catalysis in crystallo.

claim: Density between the reactant phosphate and nucleophilic water increased along with longer soaking time, indicating the generation of phosphate products.
source: Density between the reactant phosphate and nucleophilic water increased along with longer soaking time, indicating the generation of phosphate products (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is an observation from electron density maps showing time-dependent changes.

claim: During the reaction, the coordination distances of the metal ion ligands decreased 0.1–0.2 Å when Mg2+ exchanged with Na+.
source: During the reaction, the coordination distances of the metal ion ligands decreased 0.1–0.2 Å when Mg2+ exchanged with Na+, which is consistent with their preferred geometry (Cowan, 2002; Figure 2B, C).
evidence: This is a structural observation consistent with known metal ion coordination preferences.

claim: At reaction time 160 s, 45% of product had been generated.
source: At reaction time 160 s, 45% of product had been generated (Figure 2D)
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from crystallographic data.

claim: Product formation plateaued to 65% at 300 s.
source: which later plateaued to 65% at 300 s.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from crystallographic data.

claim: During the reaction process, the sugar ring of the reactant and product DNA that resides around 3 Å away from the scissile phosphate remained in a C3′-endo conformation.
source: During the reaction process, the sugar ring of the reactant and product DNA that resides around 3 Å away from the scissile phosphate, remained in a C3′-endo conformation.
evidence: This is a structural observation from crystallographic data.

claim: As Mg2+ soaking time increased from 10 to 160 s, the WatN was observed approaching the scissile phosphate.
source: As Mg2+ soaking time increased from 10 to 160 s, we observed the WatN approaching the scissile phosphate (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is a time-dependent structural observation from crystallographic data.

claim: The conserved His98 sidechain was slightly rotated as Mg2+ soaking time increased.
source: At the same time, the conserved His98 sidechain proposed to deprotonate the WatN was slightly rotated.
evidence: This is a structural observation from crystallographic data.

claim: The electron density for the Mg2+ metal ion strongly correlated (R2 = 0.97) with product formation.
source: Throughout the reaction process with Mg2+, we found that the electron density for the Mg2+ metal ion strongly correlated (R2 = 0.97) with product formation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, C)
evidence: This is a quantitative analysis of crystallographic data showing correlation.

claim: Saturation of the metal ion site may be required and sufficient for I-PpoI catalysis.
source: which may suggest that saturation of this metal ion site is required and sufficient for catalysis.
evidence: This is an inference based on the strong correlation between metal ion binding and product formation.

claim: With 500 µM Mn2+ in the reaction buffer, the reaction process and the product conformation were similar to that for Mg2+.
source: With 500 µM Mn2+ in the reaction buffer, we found that the reaction process and the product conformation were similar to that for Mg2+.
evidence: This is a comparative observation from crystallographic data with different metal ions.

claim: After 160 s Mn2+ soaking, clear anomalous signal was present at the metal ion-binding site, confirming the binding of Mn2+.
source: After 160 s Mn2+ soaking, clear anomalous signal was present at the metal ion-binding site, confirming the binding of Mn2+ (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from anomalous diffraction data.

claim: For crystal structures of I-PpoI with partial product formation, Mn2+ signal at the metal ion site correlated with product formation with a R2 of 0.98.
source: For crystal structures of I-PpoI with partial product formation, Mn2+ signal at the metal ion site correlated with product formation with a R2 of 0.98 (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a quantitative analysis of crystallographic data showing strong correlation.

claim: Apart from the single metal ion-binding site, no anomalous signal for additional Mn2+ was detected despite 200 mM Mn2+ concentration.
source: However, apart from the single metal ion-binding site, we do not detect anomalous signal for additional Mn2+, despite such high concentration of Mn2+ (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from anomalous diffraction data at high metal ion concentration.

claim: The strong correlation between product phosphate formation with Mn2+ binding and the absence of additional anomalous density peaks in heavy Mn2+ soaked crystals suggest that one and only one divalent metal ion is involved in I-PpoI DNA hydrolysis.
source: The strong correlation between product phosphate formation with Mn2+ binding and the absence of additional anomalous density peaks in heavy Mn2+ soaked crystals suggest that one and only one divalent metal ion is involved in I-PpoI DNA hydrolysis.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on multiple lines of crystallographic evidence.

claim: Product conversion remained unaffected with increasing Tl+ in solution (apart from precipitation at 50 and 100 mM Tl+).
source: Apart from precipitation that occurred at 50 and 100 mM Tl+, we found that product conversion remained unaffected with increasing Tl+ in solution (Figure 3—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from biochemical assays.

claim: Increasing Na+ concentration in solution did not increase product conversion.
source: Similarly, increasing Na+ concentration in solution did not increase product conversion (Figure 3—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from biochemical assays.

claim: Only one Tl+ was detected by its anomalous signal in the pre-reaction state.
source: In addition, only one Tl+ was detected by its anomalous signal in the pre-reaction state (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from anomalous diffraction data.

claim: Additional monovalent metal ion may not be necessary for DNA hydrolysis by I-PpoI.
source: The biochemical and structural results indicate that additional monovalent metal ion may not be necessary for DNA hydrolysis.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on biochemical and structural data.

claim: Deprotonation of the WatN is required for the nucleophilic attack and phosphodiester bond breakage during DNA hydrolysis.
source: During DNA hydrolysis, deprotonation of the WatN is required for the nucleophilic attack and phosphodiester bond breakage.
evidence: This is a mechanistic statement based on established knowledge of nucleophilic substitution reactions.

claim: His98 has been proposed to mediate proton transfer from the nucleophilic water.
source: This proton transfer has been proposed to be mediated by the highly conserved His98 (Galburt et al., 1999; Flick et al., 1998) that lies within 3 Å from the WatN.
evidence: This is a mechanistic proposal supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: I-PpoI cleavage activity increased with pH with a pKa of 8.3.
source: The DNA cleavage assay revealed that I-PpoI cleavage activity increased with pH with a pKa of 8.3 (Figure 4A)
evidence: This is an experimental observation from biochemical assays.

claim: The pKa of 8.3 for I-PpoI activity is much higher than the pKa of histidine.
source: which is much higher than the pKa of histidine
evidence: This is a comparison with known pKa values of histidine.

claim: The histidine pKa and the proton transfer process may be affected by the active site environment.
source: but the histidine pKa and the proton transfer process may be affected by the active site environment.
evidence: This is a speculation to explain the observed pKa difference.

claim: Higher pH resulted in faster product formation in crystallo.
source: Consistent with in solution experiments, higher pH resulted in faster product formation in crystallo (Figure 4B)
evidence: This is an experimental observation from in crystallo soaking experiments.

claim: Over 100 times higher concentration of Mg2+ was needed to yield 50% product in pH 6 versus pH 8.
source: Our results showed that over 100 times higher concentration of Mg2+ was needed to yield 50% product in pH 6 versus 8 (Figure 4C)
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from biochemical assays.

claim: pH affects metal-ion-dependent I-PpoI catalysis.
source: confirming that pH affects metal-ion-dependent I-PpoI catalysis.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the Mg2+ titration experiments at different pH.

claim: The reactions in crystallo at higher pH reached 50% product formation at shorter soaking times (320 s at pH 6, 160 s at pH 7, and 80 s at pH 8).
source: Likewise, the reactions in crystallo at higher pH reached 50% product formation at shorter soaking times (320 s at pH 6, 160 s at pH 7, and 80 s at pH 8, respectively).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from in crystallo experiments.

claim: The crystal structures that contained 30–35% product at pH 6 and 8 were nearly identical.
source: Interestingly, the crystal structures that contained 30–35% product at pH 6 and 8 were nearly identical (Figure 4D, E).
evidence: This is a structural comparison from crystallographic data.

claim: The positions of the His98 residue and the WatN were practically superimposable at different pH.
source: The positions of the His98 residue and the WatN were practically superimposable (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is a structural observation from crystallographic data.

claim: At all pH, Mg2+ binding strongly correlated with product formation (R2 > 0.95).
source: At all pH, Mg2+ binding strongly correlated with product formation (R2 > 0.95), suggesting that low pH reduces the overall reaction rate without altering the reaction pathway (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D, E).
evidence: This is a quantitative analysis of crystallographic data across different pH conditions.

claim: Low pH reduces the overall reaction rate without altering the reaction pathway.
source: At all pH, Mg2+ binding strongly correlated with product formation (R2 > 0.95), suggesting that low pH reduces the overall reaction rate without altering the reaction pathway
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the strong correlation at all pH values.

claim: H98A I-PpoI cleavage activity drastically dropped compared to wild-type.
source: As expected, cleavage activity of H98A I-PpoI drastically dropped.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from biochemical assays.

claim: H98A I-PpoI displayed residual activity but required a reaction time of 1 hr to be comparable to WT I-PpoI.

evidence: This is an experimental observation from biochemical assays.

claim: H98A I-PpoI behavior is similar to the H98Q mutant in previous studies.
source: similar to the H98Q mutant in previous studies (Eastberg et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a comparison with previous mutational studies, supported by citation.

claim: Varying the pH for H98A I-PpoI resulted in a sigmoidal activity curve corresponding to a pKa of 7.9.
source: Furthermore, varying the pH resulted in a sigmoidal activity curve of I-PpoI pH dependence, corresponding to a pKa of 7.9 (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from pH-dependent biochemical assays.

claim: The significantly reduced reaction rate and the shift of pH dependence suggest that His98 plays a key role in pH sensing and water deprotonation.
source: The significantly reduced reaction rate and the shift of pH dependence suggest that His98 plays a key role in pH sensing and water deprotonation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the mutational and pH-dependence data.

claim: The low but existing activity of H98A I-PpoI suggests the presence of alternative general bases for proton transfer.
source: On the other hand, the low but existing activity of H98A I-PpoI suggests the presence of alternative general bases for proton transfer.
evidence: This is an inference based on the residual activity observed in the H98A mutant.

claim: His78 resides on the nucleophile side 3.8 Å from the WatN, with a cluster of water molecules in between.
source: Another histidine (His78) resides on the nucleophile side 3.8 Å from the WatN, with a cluster of water molecules in between (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a structural observation from crystallographic data.

claim: His78 may substitute His98 as the proton acceptor.
source: We hypothesized that His78 may substitute His98 as the proton acceptor.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on structural proximity and mutational analysis.

claim: The single mutant H78A I-PpoI had an activity similar to WT.
source: The DNA cleavage assays revealed that the single mutant, H78A I-PpoI, had an activity similar to WT
evidence: This is an experimental observation from biochemical assays.

claim: The double mutant H78A/H98A I-PpoI exhibited much lower activity than that of H98A.
source: whereas the double mutant (H78A/H98A I-PpoI) exhibited much lower activity than that of H98A (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from biochemical assays.

claim: Varying the pH for H78A/H98A I-PpoI resulted in a sigmoidal activity curve that corresponded to a pKa of 8.7.
source: Furthermore, varying the pH for H78A/H98A I-PpoI resulted in a sigmoidal activity curve that corresponded to a pKa of 8.7 (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from pH-dependent biochemical assays.

claim: The results confirm the possibility of His78 as an alternative general base.
source: In consistent with previous speculations, our results confirm the possibility of His78 as an alternative general base (Eastberg et al., 2007).
evidence: This conclusion is based on the double mutant data and is consistent with previous speculations.

claim: The residual activity and pH dependence of H78A/H98A I-PpoI indicated that something else was still activating the nucleophilic water in the absence of any nearby histidine.
source: The residual activity and pH dependence of H78A/H98A I-PpoI indicated that something else was still activating the nucleophilic water in the absence of any nearby histidine.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed residual activity in the double mutant.

claim: Titrating imidazole in H98A and H78A/H98A I-PpoI partially rescued cleavage activity.
source: Furthermore, we found that titrating imidazole in H98A and H78A/H98A I-PpoI partially rescued cleavage activity (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, B)
evidence: This is an experimental observation from biochemical assays with imidazole.

claim: Imidazole rescue of activity is similar as observed in Cas9 and EndA nuclease.
source: similar as observed in Cas9 and EndA nuclease (Furuhata and Kato, 2021; Moon et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a comparison with previous studies, supported by citations.

claim: His98 is the primary proton acceptor in I-PpoI.
source: Collectively, our results indicate that His98 is the primary proton acceptor like previous simulation results (Maghsoud et al., 2023)
evidence: This conclusion is based on mutational data and is consistent with previous simulations.

claim: I-PpoI can use alternative pathways to activate the nucleophilic WatN.
source: but at the same time, I-PpoI can use alternative pathways to activate the nucleophilic WatN.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the residual activity observed in mutants and imidazole rescue experiments.

claim: The H98A I-PpoI structure looked nearly identical to the Na+ structure and previous H98A I-PpoI structure with Mg2+.
source: The structure looked nearly identical to the Na+ structure and previous H98A I-PpoI structure with Mg2+.
evidence: This is a structural comparison from crystallographic data.

claim: After soaking H98A I-PpoI crystals for 1800s in 500 µM Mn2+, the metal ion-binding site was devoid of any anomalous signal.
source: However, to our surprise, the metal ion-binding site was devoid of any anomalous signal.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from anomalous diffraction data.

claim: Increasing the Mn2+ concentration to 1 mM still did not produce anomalous density at the Me2+-binding site in H98A I-PpoI.
source: Increasing the Mn2+ concentration to 1 mM still did not produce anomalous density at the Me2+-binding site (Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from anomalous diffraction data.

claim: Metal ion binding can be altered by perturbing His98 and possibly water deprotonation.
source: The results indicate that metal ion binding can be altered by perturbing His98 and possibly water deprotonation
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the lack of metal ion binding in the H98A mutant.

claim: The metal ion-binding site and His98 exist 7 Å apart without direct interaction.
source: even though the metal ion-binding site and His98 exist 7 Å apart without direct interaction.
evidence: This is a structural observation from crystallographic data.

claim: Metal ion binding, imidazole binding, or product formation were not detected after soaking H98A I-PpoI crystals in 1 mM Mg/Mn2+ and 100 mM imidazole for 15 h.
source: Although we tried soaking the H98A I-PpoI crystals in 1 mM Mg/Mn2+ and 100 mM imidazole for 15 h, metal ion binding, imidazole binding, or product formation were not detected (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D)
evidence: This is an experimental observation from in crystallo soaking experiments.

claim: The lack of reaction in crystallo with imidazole is possibly due to the difficulty of imidazole diffusion within the lattice.
source: possibly due to the difficulty of imidazole diffusion within the lattice.
evidence: This is a speculation to explain the negative result.

claim: Perturbing the deprotonation pathway affects not only nucleophilic attack but also metal binding.
source: Our results indicate that perturbing the deprotonation pathway not only affects nucleophilic attack but also metal binding
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the H98A mutant data showing lack of metal ion binding.

claim: I-PpoI catalyzes DNA catalysis via a concerted mechanism.
source: suggesting that I-PpoI catalyzes DNA catalysis via a concerted mechanism.
evidence: This is a mechanistic conclusion based on the coupling between metal ion binding and deprotonation.

claim: Time-resolved crystallography can visualize time-dependent structural changes and elucidate mechanisms of enzyme catalysis with unparalleled detail in crystallo.
source: Time-resolved crystallography can visualize time-dependent structural changes and elucidate mechanisms of enzyme catalysis with unparalleled detail in crystallo
evidence: This is a general statement about the capabilities of time-resolved crystallography.

claim: Light-dependent enzyme reactions can be synchronously initiated by light pulses for time-resolved crystallography.
source: especially for light-dependent enzymes, in which the reactions can be synchronously initiated by light pulses (Wilson, 2022; Brändén and Neutze, 2021; Maestre-Reyna et al., 2023; Christou et al., 2023).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work on light-activated time-resolved crystallography.

claim: Metal ion diffusion-based time-resolved crystallographic techniques have uncovered rich dynamics at the active site and transient metal ion binding during catalytic processes of metal-ion-dependent DNA polymerases.
source: In complementary, recently advanced metal ion diffusion-based time-resolved crystallographic techniques have uncovered rich dynamics at the active site and transient metal ion binding during the catalytic processes of metal-ion-dependent DNA polymerases (Freudenthal et al., 2013; Gao and Yang, 2016; Nakamura et al., 2012; Vyas et al., 2015; Chim et al., 2021; Gregory et al., 2021)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies using metal ion soaking.

claim: Metal ion diffusion-based time-resolved crystallographic techniques have uncovered dynamics during catalytic processes of nucleases.
source: recently advanced metal ion diffusion-based time-resolved crystallographic techniques have uncovered rich dynamics at the active site and transient metal ion binding during the catalytic processes of...nucleases (Samara and Yang, 2018; Wu et al., 2019)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Metal ion diffusion-based time-resolved crystallographic techniques have uncovered dynamics during catalytic processes of glycosylase.
source: recently advanced metal ion diffusion-based time-resolved crystallographic techniques have uncovered rich dynamics at the active site and transient metal ion binding during the catalytic processes of...glycosylase (Demir et al., 2023).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Transient metal ions play critical roles in water deprotonation for nucleophilic attack in RNaseH.
source: In addition to metal ions captured in static structures, these transient metal ions have been shown to play critical roles in catalysis, such as water deprotonation for nucleophilic attack in RNaseH (Samara and Yang, 2018)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a specific study.

claim: Transient metal ions play critical roles in bond breakage and product stabilization in polymerases.
source: these transient metal ions have been shown to play critical roles in catalysis, such as...bond breakage and product stabilization in polymerases (Freudenthal et al., 2013; Gao and Yang, 2016; Nakamura et al., 2012; Vyas et al., 2015; Gregory et al., 2021; Reed and Suo, 2017; Chang et al., 2022)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Transient metal ions play critical roles in alignment of the substrate and nucleophilic water in MutT.
source: and alignment of the substrate and nucleophilic water in MutT (Nakamura and Yamagata, 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a specific study.

claim: The observed location of the Me2+ in I-PpoI on the leaving group side of the scissile phosphate corresponds to the Me2+B in two-metal-ion-dependent nucleases.
source: The observed location of the Me2+ on the leaving group side of the scissile phosphate corresponds to the Me2+B in two-metal-ion-dependent nucleases (Yang, 2008; Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a structural comparison with two-metal-ion nucleases, supported by citation.

claim: The metal ion in I-PpoI is coordinated by a water cluster and asparagine side chain rather than acidic aspartate and glutamic acid clusters.
source: First, it is coordinated by a water cluster and asparagine side chain (sometimes with an additional aspartate residue) rather than the acidic aspartate and glutamic acid clusters that outline the active sites of RNaseH and APE1 nuclease (Tsutakawa et al., 2013) as well as DNA polymerases (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a structural comparison with other nucleases and polymerases.

claim: In the absence of divalent Mg2+ or Mn2+, the active site including the scissile phosphate was already well aligned in I-PpoI.
source: Even in the absence of divalent Mg2+ or Mn2+, the active site including the scissile phosphate was already well aligned in I-PpoI, which is again different from RNaseH.
evidence: This is a structural observation from pre-reaction state structures.

claim: Leu116 and the beta sheet consisting of Arg61, Gln63, Lys65, and Thr67 helped to position the DNA optimally toward the active site.
source: Instead, Leu116 and the beta sheet consisting of Arg61, Gln63, Lys65, and Thr67 (Flick et al., 1998; Galburt et al., 2000) helped to position the DNA optimally toward the active site (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, C).
evidence: This is a structural observation supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Single metal ion binding is strictly correlated with product formation in all conditions tested.
source: Second, single metal ion binding is strictly correlated with product formation in all conditions, at different pH and with different mutants (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–E; Moon et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on quantitative analysis of crystallographic data across multiple conditions.

claim: The metal ion in I-PpoI is not required for substrate alignment but is essential for catalysis.
source: Thus, similar to the third metal ion in DNA polymerases and RNaseH, the metal ion in I-PpoI is not required for substrate alignment but is essential for catalysis.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on structural observations and comparison with other enzymes.

claim: The single metal ion in I-PpoI helps stabilize the transition state and reduce the electronegative buildup of DNA, thereby promoting DNA hydrolysis.
source: We suspect that the single metal ion helps stabilize the transition state and reduce the electronegative buildup of DNA, thereby promoting DNA hydrolysis.
evidence: This is a mechanistic speculation based on the observed correlation between metal ion binding and catalysis.

claim: His98 is perfectly positioned to mediate proton transfer, existing close to the nucleophilic water at 2.6 Å.
source: Existing close to the nucleophilic water at 2.6 Å, His98 is perfectly positioned to mediate the proton transfer.
evidence: This is a structural observation from crystallographic data.

claim: Due to the bulky presence of His98 and beta sheet protein residues, there is no space for an additional metal ion at the nucleophilic side.
source: Moreover, due to the bulky presence of His98 and beta sheet protein residues, there is no space for an additional metal ion at the nucleophilic side (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a structural observation explaining the absence of a second metal ion.

claim: Water deprotonation and metal ion binding appeared to be highly correlated in I-PpoI.
source: Based on our in crystallo observations, water deprotonation and metal ion binding appeared to be highly correlated (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on multiple lines of experimental evidence.

claim: Lowering the pH reduced reaction rate and slowed metal ion binding.
source: Lowering the pH not only reduced reaction rate but also slowed metal ion binding (Figure 4B, C).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from pH-dependent studies.

claim: The divalent metal ion may be sensitive to the charge potential of the substrate scissile phosphate, which may be indirectly affected by the deprotonated state of the nucleophilic water.
source: As there is no direct interaction between His98 and the Me2+-binding site, the divalent metal ion may be sensitive to the charge potential of the substrate scissile phosphate, which may be indirectly affected by the deprotonated state of the nucleophilic water.
evidence: This is a mechanistic speculation to explain the coupling between metal ion binding and deprotonation.

claim: Binding of the divalent metal ion may alter the local electrostatic environment and affect His98 deprotonation.
source: Conversely, binding of the divalent metal ion may alter the local electrostatic environment and affect His98 deprotonation.
evidence: This is a mechanistic speculation about the reciprocal relationship between metal binding and deprotonation.

claim: Previous molecular dynamics simulation of Cas9 suggested that the histidine pKa is highly sensitive to active site changes.
source: Consistently, previous molecular dynamics simulation of Cas9 has suggested that the histidine pKa is highly sensitive to active site changes (Nierzwicki et al., 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous computational study.

claim: Without a proper proton acceptor, the metal ion may be prone for dissociation without the reaction proceeding.
source: Without a proper proton acceptor, the metal ion may be prone for dissociation without the reaction proceeding, and thus stable Mg2+ binding was not observed in crystallo without His98 (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation of the H98A mutant data.

claim: Optimal alignment of the metal ion and WatN within the active site leads to irreversible bond breakage.
source: On the other hand, optimal alignment of the metal ion and WatN within the active site, labeled as metal-binding state, leads to irreversible bond breakage (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is a mechanistic conclusion based on the experimental observations.

claim: The experimental observations suggest a concerted mechanism for one-metal-ion promoted DNA hydrolysis.
source: In summary, our experimental observations suggest a concerted mechanism for one-metal-ion promoted DNA hydrolysis
evidence: This is the main mechanistic conclusion of the study based on all experimental data.
